standard.title: Quantifying and Comparing Collections
standard.description: quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting and explain or demonstrate reasoning
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have informal counting experience and can name numbers. They are developing reliable one-to-one correspondence. They have not yet systematically applied counting principles (each object counted once, arrangement does not affect quantity, last number = total) or used counting to compare and justify.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students quantify and compare collections to at least 20 using counting, demonstrating one-to-one correspondence and cardinality, and explain or demonstrate their reasoning.

nodes.label: Counting principles
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can count a collection of objects accurately, demonstrating that each object is counted once, arrangement does not affect quantity, and the last number counted tells how many.
nodes.minimum_width: Count a collection of up to 10 objects in a fixed arrangement accurately, demonstrating one-to-one correspondence; state the total when asked 'How many?'
nodes.typical_width: Count collections of objects to at least 20 in varying arrangements; demonstrate that rearranging objects does not change how many there are; apply counting principles across different types of objects and counting contexts (physical, virtual, moving objects).
wider: Use body-tallying systems from First Nations Peoples of Australia that use body parts and one-to-one correspondence to count to 20
Compare how different cultural tools (e.g. an abacus, Chinese hand gestures) represent the counting process — connecting to the universal counting principles

response_modes.reason: Students commonly misapply counting principles in specific situations — they may count correctly in a line but miscount scattered objects, or not understand that rearranging a counted set doesn't change the total. Encountering collections in varied arrangements resolves the conservation misconception more effectively than repeated practice with a single arrangement type.

One-to-one correspondence with physical objects requires procedural care — students commonly double-count or skip objects. Repeated counting practice across many collections builds the tracking precision needed before comparison tasks.

nodes.hinge_reason: Nodes 2 and 3 depend on accurate counting. Students who misapply counting principles — skipping objects, double-counting, or believing arrangement changes quantity — produce wrong counts, making purposeful counting and comparison unreliable. Both the conservation misconception and procedural tracking errors cascade through all downstream counting tasks.
success_criteria: Student accurately counts a collection of 10–20 objects in a scattered arrangement with no double-counting or skipping
Student states the total correctly when asked 'How many?' after counting
Student demonstrates (without recounting) that rearranging a counted set does not change the total

nodes.label: Counting for a purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use counting to determine a quantity needed for a practical purpose, applying one-to-one correspondence.
nodes.minimum_width: Count the members of a group and use that count to collect the right number of items for the group.
nodes.typical_width: Use counting and one-to-one correspondence to quantify items required for a practical purpose (e.g. collecting one item per person, setting a table, distributing materials); explain reasoning about why the count gives the right number.
wider: Investigate quantifying situations that involve multiple sets (e.g. collecting two items for each person) and use counting to determine the total needed
Explore First Nations Australians' counting contexts where quantity serves a practical purpose — e.g. gathering enough for a group
success_criteria: Student uses counting to determine the correct number of items needed for a group and collects that quantity
Student explains why their count gives the right answer (connecting count to purpose)

nodes.label: Comparing collections using counting
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare the size of two or more collections using counting and justify which has more or fewer.
nodes.minimum_width: Count two collections and compare them, stating which has more and how they know.
nodes.typical_width: Count and compare collections of up to 20 objects; justify which collection has more or fewer using the count; apply comparison to practical situations (e.g. 'Do we have enough scissors for everyone?').
wider: Compare three or more collections, ordering them from fewest to most and justifying the order with counts
Investigate comparison situations where counting is needed because subitising is not reliable (collections greater than 5) — connecting comparison strategy to quantity size
Explore how different cultures represent and compare quantities — connecting to the universality of counting as a comparison tool

response_modes.reason: Students commonly compare collections by visual impression (which pile looks bigger) rather than counting. The reasoning scaffold here is: count each collection, then compare the counts. Getting students to explicitly articulate this two-step process — count first, then compare — is the key teaching move at this node.

Comparison integrates counting principles (node 1) and purposeful counting (node 2) into a reasoning task. Students must count accurately AND use the counts to draw a justified conclusion about relative size. This coordination is the endpoint demand.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparison contexts that involve practical purposes (enough for the group? who has more?) give advancing students meaningful reasoning tasks. Multi-collection comparison and ordering extend the concept without leaving the year band.
success_criteria: Student counts two collections of up to 20 objects accurately and correctly states which has more
Student explains reasoning — naming the counts of both collections and using them to justify the comparison
